```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
logger::log_threshold(logger::WARN, namespace = "pdmS7")
pal <- c(blue = "#236b83", orange = "#a26421", green = "#5b8c3a", grey = "#9aa7b0",
         dark = "#444444", purple = "#8a3b6b", red = "#b23b3b")
fill <- c(blue = "#e3eef2", orange = "#f6ebe0", green = "#e7f0e1", grey = "#eef1f3",
          purple = "#f1e5ec", red = "#f5e2e2")

# Drawing helpers for the flow diagrams: a blank 0-1 canvas, boxes, diamonds and arrows.
canvas <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
  plot.window(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1))
}
box <- function(x, y, label, w = 0.17, h = 0.12, col = "blue", cex = 0.78, font = 1) {
  rect(x - w / 2, y - h / 2, x + w / 2, y + h / 2, col = fill[[col]], border = pal[[col]],
       lwd = 1.6)
  text(x, y, label, cex = cex, font = font, col = pal[["dark"]])
}
diamond <- function(x, y, label, w = 0.2, h = 0.16, col = "orange", cex = 0.74) {
  polygon(c(x - w / 2, x, x + w / 2, x), c(y, y + h / 2, y, y - h / 2), col = fill[[col]],
          border = pal[[col]], lwd = 1.6)
  text(x, y, label, cex = cex, col = pal[["dark"]])
}
arrow <- function(x0, y0, x1, y1, label = NULL, pos = 3, col = "dark") {
  arrows(x0, y0, x1, y1, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.4, col = pal[[col]])
  if (!is.null(label)) {
    text((x0 + x1) / 2, (y0 + y1) / 2, label, pos = pos, cex = 0.72, col = pal[[col]],
         offset = 0.3)
  }
}
```

Automatic calibration means letting the computer find the model parameters that make the
simulated river match the measured one. Done well, it is faster and more repeatable than
calibrating by hand, and every step can be checked. Done carelessly, it produces a model that
scores well and is wrong where it matters.

This article walks through a whole calibration in pdmS7, from the data to sign-off, in plain
English and with diagrams. It explains what each step does and why it is there. The detail of
each step is in its own article, linked as you go.

# The whole journey

```{r overview, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="A calibration from start to finish. Every step writes an entry to the project log."}
canvas()
top <- 0.74
bottom <- 0.36
xs <- c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9)
steps_top <- c("1. Register\nthe data", "2. Look at\nthe events", "3. Choose the\nstructure",
               "4. Calibrate\nin stages", "5. Run the\nchecks")
steps_bottom <- c("10. Sign-off", "9. Test on the\nwettest years", "8. Validate on\nunseen years",
                  "7. Propose the\ncandidate", "6. Look at the\nfloods yourself")
for (i in 1:5) box(xs[i], top, steps_top[i])
for (i in 1:5) box(xs[i], bottom, steps_bottom[i], col = if (i == 1) "green" else "blue")
for (i in 1:4) arrow(xs[i] + 0.085, top, xs[i + 1] - 0.085, top)
arrow(xs[5], top - 0.06, xs[5], bottom + 0.06)
for (i in 5:2) arrow(xs[i] - 0.085, bottom, xs[i - 1] + 0.085, bottom)
rect(0.02, 0.06, 0.98, 0.16, col = fill[["grey"]], border = pal[["grey"]])
text(0.5, 0.11, "The project log: every step written down, who did it, when, and why",
     cex = 0.85, col = pal[["dark"]])
arrows(0.5, 0.29, 0.5, 0.17, length = 0.06, lty = 2, col = pal[["grey"]])
segments(0.9, top + 0.06, 0.9, top + 0.15, col = pal[["red"]], lwd = 1.4)
segments(0.9, top + 0.15, 0.5, top + 0.15, col = pal[["red"]], lwd = 1.4)
arrows(0.5, top + 0.15, 0.5, top + 0.06, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.4, col = pal[["red"]])
text(0.7, top + 0.15, "if the checks fail, go back", pos = 3, cex = 0.72, col = pal[["red"]],
     offset = 0.3)
```

| Step | What happens | In pdmS7 |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Register the data | Rain, evaporation and flow are stored in the project, with the years for warming up, calibrating and validating | `start_calibration_project()`, `register_data()` |
| 2. Look at the events | The floods are found in the record, and the doubtful ones set aside | `find_events()`, `screen_events()` |
| 3. Choose the structure | Which version of the model to fit: its soil store, recharge and groundwater store | `select_structure()`, `recommend_structure()` |
| 4. Calibrate in stages | The search for parameters, one group at a time | `pdm_stages()`, `log_staged_calibration()` |
| 5. Run the checks | Warning signs the score hides: parameters at their limits, floods late or low | `calibration_checks()` |
| 6. Look at the floods | The largest events side by side, adjusted by eye if need be | `event_workbench()`, the app's Events tab |
| 7. Propose | The chosen calibration is put forward, with the reasons | `propose_candidate()` |
| 8. Validate | The candidate is scored on years no calibration saw | `validate_candidate()` |
| 9. Test | The wettest years, held back from the start, are revealed | `test_candidate()` |
| 10. Sign-off | A Steward reviews the log and signs | `sign_off_project()` |

Steps 3 to 6 often go round more than once: the checks find a problem, and the hydrologist goes
back to the structure, the stages or the rain.

# Step 1: the data and the years

A calibration needs rain, potential evaporation and measured flow on the same time steps. Once
registered, the data are copied into the project and fingerprinted, so that later steps can
prove which data they used.

The record is then divided:

```{r timeline, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.6, fig.cap="How the record is divided. The wettest years are held back from calibration and validation, and revealed only at the end."}
canvas()
years <- 2008:2025
x_of <- function(y) 0.05 + 0.9 * (y - 2008) / 18
band <- function(from, to, y, col, label, at = (from + to) / 2) {
  rect(x_of(from), y - 0.08, x_of(to), y + 0.08, col = fill[[col]], border = pal[[col]],
       lwd = 1.4)
  text(x_of(at), y, label, cex = 0.8, col = pal[["dark"]])
}
band(2008, 2010, 0.6, "grey", "warm-up")
band(2010, 2019, 0.6, "blue", "calibration", at = 2012)
band(2019, 2025.5, 0.6, "green", "validation", at = 2023.2)
for (held in c(2016, 2020)) {
  rect(x_of(held), 0.52, x_of(held + 1), 0.68, col = fill[["orange"]], border = pal[["orange"]],
       lwd = 2)
}
text(x_of(2016.5), 0.3, "held-back wettest years (orange): scored only by the final test",
     cex = 0.8, col = pal[["orange"]])
segments(x_of(2008), 0.82, x_of(2025.5), 0.82, col = pal[["grey"]])
for (y in seq(2008, 2024, by = 4)) {
  segments(x_of(y), 0.8, x_of(y), 0.84, col = pal[["grey"]])
  text(x_of(y), 0.9, y, cex = 0.75, col = pal[["dark"]])
}
```

- **Warm-up.** The model starts with its stores at a guess. A year or two of running lets them
  settle before anything is scored.
- **Calibration.** The years the search fits.
- **Validation.** Later years the search never sees. A model that does well here has learned
  the catchment, not the quirks of the calibration years.
- **The wettest years, held back.** The years with the largest floods are taken out of both
  windows at the start and scored only at the end. They test whether the model holds up on
  floods larger than anything it was fitted to, which is what a flood warning model is for.

See [Larger floods](extrapolation.html) for the held-back years and [Getting started with
data](data-preparation.html) for preparing the files.

# Step 2: what the search does

The model has a handful of parameters: how much water the soil holds, how fast the surface and
groundwater stores drain, and so on. The search tries sets of values, runs the model over the
calibration years with each, and keeps the one whose flow is closest to the measured flow.

```{r search, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="The search loop. It runs hundreds or thousands of times, from several starting points."}
canvas()
box(0.15, 0.55, "Try a set of\nparameter values", col = "blue")
box(0.4, 0.55, "Run the model\nover the record", col = "blue")
box(0.65, 0.55, "Score the flow\nagainst the gauge", col = "blue")
diamond(0.87, 0.55, "Better than\nthe best so far?", w = 0.2, h = 0.22)
arrow(0.235, 0.55, 0.315, 0.55)
arrow(0.485, 0.55, 0.565, 0.55)
arrow(0.735, 0.55, 0.77, 0.55)
segments(0.87, 0.66, 0.87, 0.85, lwd = 1.4, col = pal[["dark"]])
segments(0.87, 0.85, 0.15, 0.85, lwd = 1.4, col = pal[["dark"]])
arrows(0.15, 0.85, 0.15, 0.61, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.4, col = pal[["dark"]])
text(0.5, 0.88, "keep it if so; choose the next values from what has been learnt", cex = 0.75,
     col = pal[["dark"]])
arrow(0.87, 0.44, 0.87, 0.24, "no more\nprogress", pos = 4)
box(0.87, 0.17, "Best set found", col = "green", w = 0.18, h = 0.1)
text(0.4, 0.2, paste("Bounds: each parameter may only move within a\nsensible range.",
                     "Starts: the loop is run from\nseveral starting points, in case one",
                     "gets stuck."), cex = 0.75, col = pal[["dark"]])
```

Four things shape the search:

- **The bounds.** Each parameter may only move within a range a hydrologist would accept, from
  a table of sensible limits. A parameter that ends pressed against its limit is a warning
  sign (step 5).
- **The score.** Usually the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE): 1 is a perfect match, 0 is no
  better than always predicting the average flow. Other scores weight low flows, volumes, or
  floods (see [Scoring a simulation](scoring.html)).
- **The method.** The default feels for the slope of the ground and walks downhill (L-BFGS-B):
  fast and reliable when the score changes smoothly. Where it changes in steps, as when
  counting floods or timing peaks to the hour, a method that tries points instead (DDS) is
  used.
- **The starts.** The ground may have several valleys. Starting the search from several
  places, and keeping the best result, guards against settling in a poor one.

[Automatic calibration, explained](auto-calibration.html) shows each of these at work.

# Step 3: choosing the structure

Before the numbers come the shape of the model: which kind of soil store, recharge and
groundwater store. pdmS7 offers several of each. `recommend_structure()` chooses one part at a
time, in the order the record can best answer:

```{r structure, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="Choosing the structure one part at a time. Each part is chosen by the same rule, and the reason is written to the log."}
canvas()
box(0.12, 0.72, "Recharge rule\n(standard, split,\ndemand)", h = 0.18)
box(0.37, 0.72, "Soil store\n(Pareto, rectangular,\nlognormal ...)", h = 0.18)
box(0.62, 0.72, "Groundwater store\n(cubic, linear,\nexponential ...)", h = 0.18)
box(0.87, 0.72, "Recommended\nstructure", col = "green", h = 0.18)
arrow(0.205, 0.72, 0.285, 0.72)
arrow(0.455, 0.72, 0.535, 0.72)
arrow(0.705, 0.72, 0.785, 0.72)
text(0.37, 0.93, "each part: fit every option, score on the validation years", cex = 0.78,
     col = pal[["dark"]])
box(0.13, 0.32, "Set aside any option\nwith a parameter\nat a limit", col = "red", w = 0.2,
    h = 0.17)
diamond(0.43, 0.32, "Is the one in use\nwithin 0.02 of\nthe best score?", w = 0.26, h = 0.26)
box(0.8, 0.43, "Keep it", col = "green", w = 0.28, h = 0.1)
box(0.8, 0.2, "Of those within 0.02: the best\nfloods, then fewest parameters", w = 0.28,
    h = 0.13)
arrow(0.23, 0.32, 0.3, 0.32)
arrow(0.56, 0.36, 0.66, 0.43, "yes", pos = 3)
arrow(0.56, 0.28, 0.66, 0.2, "no", pos = 1)
```

Tests on made-up catchments, where the true structure was known, showed what a record can
tell apart. The recharge rule was found every time, by a clear margin. The groundwater store
was found only by margins too small to survive real data, so the rule keeps the standard store
unless another is clearly better. See [Choosing a model structure](choosing-structure.html) and
[What limits automatic calibration](calibration-study.html).

# Step 4: calibrating in stages

A hydrologist calibrating by hand does not move everything at once. They settle the water
balance first, then the shape of the floods, then make a final adjustment. The staged
calibration does the same:

```{r stages, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="The four stages. Each starts from where the last left off. Stage 4 is optional, for models whose floods matter most."}
canvas()
xs <- c(0.13, 0.38, 0.63, 0.88)
titles <- c("1. Volume and\nbaseflow", "2. Fast\nresponse", "3. Polish", "4. Events\n(optional)")
moves <- c("rainfall factor,\nsoil store, recharge,\ngroundwater",
           "surface stores,\nsoil store shape b", "everything,\nover the full ranges",
           "surface stores, b,\ntime delay")
scores <- c("log NSE + volume:\nlow flows and\nthe water balance",
            "NSE: the peaks\nand their timing",
            "NSE", "the largest floods:\nshape, peak size,\ntiming")
cols <- c("blue", "blue", "blue", "orange")
for (i in 1:4) {
  box(xs[i], 0.8, titles[i], col = cols[i], w = 0.2, h = 0.14, font = 2)
  box(xs[i], 0.52, moves[i], col = "grey", w = 0.21, h = 0.17, cex = 0.72)
  box(xs[i], 0.22, scores[i], col = "green", w = 0.21, h = 0.17, cex = 0.72)
}
for (i in 1:3) arrow(xs[i] + 0.1, 0.8, xs[i + 1] - 0.1, 0.8)
text(0.005, 0.52, "moves", srt = 90, cex = 0.8, col = pal[["dark"]])
text(0.005, 0.22, "scored by", srt = 90, cex = 0.8, col = pal[["dark"]])
```

- **Stage 1** fits the parts that control how much water there is and how the river falls
  between storms, judged on log flows so that the floods do not dominate.
- **Stage 2** fits the parts that shape each flood, with the water balance held.
- **Stage 3** lets everything move together over its full range, to fix anything the first two
  missed. It must be free to move far: a polish kept close to stage 2 can lock in a wrong first
  stage.
- **Stage 4**, the events stage, refits the flood-shaping parts and the time delay on the
  largest floods alone. Over a long record most hours are quiet, so a model can score well with
  every peak late and low; this stage puts the floods first. See [Getting the floods
  right](floods.html).

# Step 5: the checks

A good score is not enough. Before accepting a calibration, `calibration_checks()` asks the
questions the score hides:

```{r checks, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5, fig.cap="The checks after a calibration, in order. Each failure points back to a different step."}
canvas()
box(0.12, 0.88, "Calibrated\nmodel", col = "green", w = 0.16, h = 0.1)
diamond(0.4, 0.88, "Any parameter\nat a limit?", w = 0.22, h = 0.16)
diamond(0.4, 0.6, "Largest floods:\npeaks and timing\nacceptable?", w = 0.24, h = 0.2)
diamond(0.4, 0.3, "Validation close\nto calibration?", w = 0.22, h = 0.16)
box(0.4, 0.07, "Propose as candidate", col = "green", w = 0.24, h = 0.09)
arrow(0.2, 0.88, 0.29, 0.88)
arrow(0.4, 0.8, 0.4, 0.7, "no", pos = 4)
arrow(0.4, 0.5, 0.4, 0.38, "yes", pos = 4)
arrow(0.4, 0.22, 0.4, 0.115, "yes", pos = 4)
box(0.8, 0.88, "The structure is being bent\nto fit: question it (step 3),\nor the bounds",
    col = "red", w = 0.3, h = 0.14)
box(0.8, 0.6, "Add the events stage (step 4),\nlook at the floods (step 6),\nor check the rain",
    col = "red", w = 0.3, h = 0.14)
box(0.8, 0.3, "Fitted to quirks of the\ncalibration years, or the\nrecord changed: review",
    col = "red", w = 0.3, h = 0.14)
arrow(0.51, 0.88, 0.65, 0.88, "yes", pos = 3)
arrow(0.52, 0.6, 0.65, 0.6, "no", pos = 3)
arrow(0.51, 0.3, 0.65, 0.3, "no", pos = 3)
```

- **A parameter at its limit** is the clearest warning sign. It means the search wanted to go
  further than a sensible value, usually to make up for something the structure cannot do. In
  one real catchment, three of seven parameters at their limits came with a score of 0.90 and
  the largest flood 47% low and 16 hours late.
- **The largest floods** in each window: the median peak error, timing error and how many peaks
  fall within 20%. Floods the rain gauges plainly missed, or rises lost in a high baseflow, are
  set aside first.
- **Validation against calibration.** Some fall in score on unseen years is normal. A large
  fall means the model has learned the calibration years rather than the catchment.

# Step 6: looking at the floods yourself

Scores summarise; they do not show. The events workbench draws the largest floods side by
side, before and after a change, and redraws them in a fraction of a second as sliders move in
the app's Events tab. A setting the hydrologist believes is saved as a trial, with a verdict
and the reasons. Judgement stays with the hydrologist, and the log records it. See [Logging a
manual calibration](calibration-log.html).

# Steps 7 to 10: candidate, validation, test, sign-off

```{r endgame, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.6, fig.cap="The last steps. Each is a separate, signed entry in the log."}
canvas()
xs <- c(0.12, 0.37, 0.62, 0.87)
labels <- c("Propose a\ncandidate", "Validate on the\nunseen years",
            "Test on the held-back\nwettest years",
            "Steward\nsigns off")
for (i in 1:4) box(xs[i], 0.55, labels[i], col = if (i == 4) "green" else "blue", w = 0.2,
                   h = 0.3)
for (i in 1:3) arrow(xs[i] + 0.1, 0.55, xs[i + 1] - 0.1, 0.55)
text(0.5, 0.12, "The validation and test scores are written down before anyone sees the next.",
     cex = 0.78, col = pal[["dark"]])
```

The candidate is proposed first, then validated, then tested, in that order and only once
each. A model cannot be quietly re-tuned after its test has been seen, because the log shows the
order in which things happened. The Steward reads the log, checks the reasoning at each step,
and signs. See [the Steward's guide](steward-guide.html).

# Everything is written down

Every step above writes an entry to the project log: what was done, the data and settings used,
the scores, who did it, when and why. Each entry carries a checksum of the one before, so the
chain cannot be edited without it showing.

```{r chain, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.4, fig.cap="The log as a chain of entries. Each entry carries a checksum of the one before."}
canvas()
labels <- c("project\nstarted", "data\nregistered", "structure\nselected", "stage 1",
            "stage 2", "stage 3", "candidate", "validation", "test", "sign-off")
xs <- seq(0.06, 0.94, length.out = length(labels))
for (i in seq_along(labels)) {
  box(xs[i], 0.55, labels[i], col = if (i == length(labels)) "green" else "grey", w = 0.085,
      h = 0.36, cex = 0.66)
}
for (i in 1:(length(labels) - 1)) arrow(xs[i] + 0.043, 0.55, xs[i + 1] - 0.043, 0.55)
text(0.5, 0.12, "each link: a checksum of the entry before", cex = 0.78, col = pal[["dark"]])
```

Here is a real, if small, calibration run through the steps, and the log it leaves:

```{r live, results="hide"}
rain <- synthetic_rain("2020-10-01", years = 2, dt = 1, seed = 3)
forcing <- data.frame(time = rain$time, rain = rain$rain, pet = rain$pet)
truth <- pdm_presets("standard")
truth$area_km2 <- 30
truth$td <- 2
model <- pdm_from_config(truth)
observed <- run_pdm(model, forcing, initial_state_from_flow(model, 0.5, 0.7))$output$q_m3s
options(pdmS7.user = "A Hydrologist", pdmS7.role = "custodian")
project <- file.path(tempdir(), "journey")
unlink(project, recursive = TRUE)
start_calibration_project(project, "Example Brook", "00002", "Journey article", 30,
                          "An Owner", "A Steward")
register_data(project, forcing, observed, calibration = c("2021-01-01", "2022-03-31 23:00"),
              validation = c("2022-04-01", "2022-09-30 23:00"), wettest_years = 0)
start <- pdm_presets("standard")
start$area_km2 <- 30
structure <- select_structure(project, start, "Standard PDM to start from")
fits <- log_staged_calibration(project, structure$id, "Four stages, with the events stage.",
                               stages = pdm_stages(start, events = TRUE, event_budget = 60),
                               starts = 1, seed = 1, control = list(maxit = 15))
propose_candidate(project, fits[[length(fits)]]$id, "Final stage of the staged calibration.")
validate_candidate(project, "Validation year.")
```

```{r live-log}
entries <- read_project(project)$entries
entries[, c("id", "type")]
checks <- calibration_checks(project, top = 5)
checks$parameters[, c("path", "value", "lower", "upper", "at_bound")]
checks$summary[, c("period", "events", "median_peak_error", "median_timing_error_h")]
```

Each row is one entry, from the start of the project to the validation of the candidate; the
four automatic calibration entries are the four stages. In the parameter table, `at_bound` is
empty (`NA`) when a parameter sits clear of its limits, and reads `lower` or `upper` when it
does not; here none does. The largest floods in every window peak within a few percent of the
measured peaks, and in the same hour.

One number is a reminder of what a good fit does not prove. The events stage found a time delay
of `r sprintf("%.1f", checks$parameters$value[checks$parameters$path == "td"])` hours, against
the true 2 used to make the record. The two surface stores came out at
`r sprintf("%.1f", checks$parameters$value[checks$parameters$path == "surface.k1"])` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", checks$parameters$value[checks$parameters$path == "surface.k2"])` hours,
against a true 2 and 4: the same two stores the other way round, which give the same flood,
with the shorter delay making up the difference. The floods come out right; the parameters
behind them are not unique. This is why the checks look
at the floods themselves, and why [What limits automatic calibration](calibration-study.html)
matters before reading too much into any one value.

# Many catchments at once

The same journey can be run over many catchments with `calibrate_batch()`, which runs each
catchment's project through the stages, survives interruptions, and resumes where it stopped.
The checks and the structure choice then become questions across the sample: which
catchments failed which check, and which structure won where. See [Calibrating many
catchments](many-catchments.html).
